title: Genesis 17. The Cup Sealed in Flesh.
edition: AID Genesis, Layer 1 (the steward's manuscript); narration: Kristin voice (public domain)
level_note: text follows the narration phrase by phrase
verse_numbers: none in this text; none shown
phrases: Genesis 17. The Cup Sealed in Flesh.
Abram is ninety-nine years old.
Thirteen years have passed since Ishmael was born.
Thirteen years of silence in the text.
No voice.
No vision.
No altar.
The Cup that was cut in chapter fifteen and filled by arrangement in chapter sixteen has sat in a house with a son who was not the promise and a wife who is still barren.
Then God appears.
I am El Shaddai.
Walk before Me and be blameless.
I will make My covenant between Me and you,
and will multiply you exceedingly.
Abram falls on his face.
God speaks.
The covenant that was cut in blood in chapter fifteen is now spoken as identity.
No more walking from Ur.
No more sojourning without a name.
God changes him.
Your name shall no longer be Abram.
Your name shall be Abraham,
for I have made you the father of a multitude of nations.
I will make you exceedingly fruitful.
I will make nations of you.
Kings shall come from you.
I will establish My covenant between Me and you and your offspring after you throughout their generations,
an everlasting covenant,
to be God to you and to your offspring after you.
I will give you the land of your sojourning,
all the land of Canaan, for an everlasting possession.
And I will be their God.
The names change because the identity changes.
Abram, exalted father, becomes Abraham, father of a multitude.
The man who had one son born of arrangement is renamed as a father of nations.
The Cup is not being refilled.
It is being re-formed.
The vessel that carried the promise under an old name now carries it under a new one.
Then God gives the sign.
Every male among you shall be circumcised.
You shall be circumcised in the flesh of your foreskin.
It shall be a sign of the covenant between Me and you.
He who is eight days old shall be circumcised,
every male throughout your generations,
whether born in the house or bought with money.
My covenant shall be in your flesh for an everlasting covenant.
The uncircumcised male who is not circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin,
that soul shall be cut off from his people.
He has broken My covenant.
The Cup is sealed in flesh.
Not on stone.
Not on paper.
Not on a mountain or a tower.
On the body.
The covenant that was cut between animals in chapter fifteen is now written on the body of every male who belongs to it.
The sign is placed where life enters the body,
at the organ of generation,
at the place where the promise of offspring must be fulfilled.
The Cup that holds the promise of a multitude is sealed at the point where that multitude begins.
Then God speaks of Sarah.
Your wife, you shall not call her Sarai.
Her name shall be Sarah.
I will bless her.
And I will give you a son by her.
I will bless her.
She shall be a mother of nations.
Kings of peoples shall come from her.
Sarai becomes Sarah.
The woman who was barren is renamed as a mother of nations.
The wife who gave her servant to produce what she could not is now told:
you will produce it yourself.
The Cup that was filled by arrangement in chapter sixteen is now promised to be filled by God in chapter seventeen.
The same body that was bypassed is now chosen.
Abraham falls on his face and laughs.
He says in his heart:
Shall a child be born to a man who is a hundred years old?
Shall Sarah, who is ninety years old, give birth?
He laughs.
The man who believed God in chapter fifteen,
and it was counted to him as righteousness,
now laughs at the promise when it becomes specific.
The faith that could count stars stumbles at a ninety-year-old womb.
The Cup that was received by faith is now met with laughter.
Not rebellion.
Not arrangement.
Laughter.
The gap between what God promises and what Abraham can imagine is so wide that the only response is to fall down and laugh.
Then Abraham says: Oh, that Ishmael might live before You.
The father who has held Ishmael for thirteen years offers him to God.
The son of arrangement, the one who was not the promise,
is the son Abraham knows.
The son who is the promise, Isaac, does not yet exist.
Abraham asks God to accept what he has instead of what God has promised.
God answers: No.
But Sarah your wife shall bear you a son.
You shall call his name Isaac.
I will establish My covenant with him,
an everlasting covenant for his offspring after him.
Isaac.
he laughs.
The son of the promise is named after the father's laughter.
The child who will carry the covenant bears the name of the moment Abraham could not believe the covenant would come.
The Cup that was met with laughter is carried by a son named Laughter.
As for Ishmael, I have heard you.
I have blessed him.
I will make him fruitful.
I will multiply him exceedingly.
He shall father twelve princes.
I will make him a great nation.
Ishmael is blessed.
The son of arrangement is not rejected.
God heard, the name means God hears, and God answers.
Ishmael will be great.
Twelve princes.
A nation.
Fruitfulness.
Multiplication.
Everything the arrangement was meant to produce, God gives it.
But the covenant does not go through him.
But My covenant I will establish with Isaac,
whom Sarah shall bear to you at this set time in the next year.
The Cup of arrangement is blessed but not chosen.
The Cup of promise is chosen but not yet born.
Ishmael receives fruit.
Isaac receives the covenant.
The distinction is not cruelty, it is purpose.
God's promise was never about quantity alone.
It was about a line.
A thread.
A Cup that carries something more than offspring,
that carries the word God spoke when He walked alone through the pieces.
God finishes speaking.
He goes up from Abraham.
Abraham takes Ishmael his son, every male born in his house,
every male bought with money, and circumcises them that very day,
as God had said to him.
Abraham is ninety-nine when he is circumcised.
Ishmael is thirteen.
All the men of his house are circumcised with him.
The seal is applied immediately.
Not when Isaac is born.
Not when Sarah conceives.
Not when the promise becomes visible.
Today.
Before the son exists, before the womb opens,
before the laughter becomes flesh,
Abraham marks every male in his household with the sign of a covenant that has not yet produced what it promised.
The Cup is sealed in flesh.
The names are changed.
The son of laughter is named.
The son of arrangement is blessed.
The ninety-year-old woman who has been barren for her entire life is told she will give birth within a year.
And a hundred-year-old man and a thirteen-year-old boy and every male in the household lie down that night with a wound in their flesh that says:
the promise is real, even when it has not yet arrived.
What was cut in blood between animals in chapter fifteen is now written on bodies in chapter seventeen.
What was spoken by voice in chapter twelve is now sealed in flesh in chapter seventeen.
What was met with laughter in the heart is now named as a son who will carry it.
The Cup holds.
The wound holds it.
